'''''Cicuta douglasii''''', the '''western water hemlock''', is a very poisonous [[perennial plant]] in the family [[Apiaceae]]. 

== Description ==
[[File:Cicuta douglasii & Conium maculatum 1459205.jpg|thumb|The leaves of ''Cicuta douglasii'' (left), along with those of ''[[Conium maculatum]]'' (poison hemlock); both species are extremely poisonous.]]

The plant's roots are thick and [[tuber]]ous, with many smaller tubers on the main one,<ref name="block">{{cite web |author=Block, N. (n.d.). |date=2005-07-13 |title=''Cicuta douglasii'' (DC.) Coult. & Rose |url=https://www.usask.ca/agriculture/plantsci/classes/range/cicuta.html}}</ref> allowing survival in wet conditions. The stem is {{convert|0.5–2|m|ft|sp=us|frac=2}} tall with purplish spots. The inner tubers and stem bases can have horizontal chambers useful for identification.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Spellenberg |first=Richard |url=https://archive.org/details/nationalaudubons00spel/page/337/ |title=National Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers: Western Region |publisher=Knopf |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-375-40233-3 |edition=rev |page=337 |orig-date=1979}}</ref> The [[leaves]] are alternate and compound pinnate; the secondary veins of the leaflets end at the bases instead of the tips of the teeth.<ref name="agfood">{{cite web |publisher=Saskatchewan Agriculture, Food and Rural Revitalization |date=2005-07-13 |title=Western Water Hemlock {{!}} ''Cicuta douglasii'' |url=http://www.agr.gov.sk.ca/DOCS/crops/integrated_pest_management/weed_identification_broadleaf_weeds/whemlock.asp |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051028235957/http://www.agr.gov.sk.ca/DOCS/crops/integrated_pest_management/weed_identification_broadleaf_weeds/whemlock.asp |archive-date=2005-10-28}}</ref><ref name="pojar">{{cite book |last1=Pojar |first1=Jim |last2=MacKinnon |first2=Andrew |date=2004 |orig-date=1994 |title=Plants of the Pacific Northwest Coast: Washington, Oregon, British Columbia & Alaska (Rev. ed.)|location=Vancouver, BC |publisher=Lone Pine Publishing |page=215 |isbn=978-1-55105-530-5}}</ref> The leaflets are {{Convert|3–10|cm|sp=us|frac=4}} long and {{cvt|1–2|cm|frac=4}} wide, with jagged edges.<ref name="block" /><ref name=":0" /> Its [[inflorescence]]s are compound umbels about {{cvt|12.5|cm|frac=2}} across,<ref name=":0" /> with many small, white flowers,<ref name="block" /> which have two seeds each. The seeds germinate in spring, and flowers mature near the end of June and beginning of July.<ref name="block" /> [[Seed dispersal]] is by means of wind, water, machinery, clothing, and through transported soil.<ref name="weedsbc">{{cite web |website=Weeds BC |date=2005-07-13 |title=Water hemlock, ''Cicuta douglasii'' |url=http://www.weedsbc.ca/weed_desc/water_hem.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020730224529/http://www.weedsbc.ca/weed_desc/water_hem.html |archive-date=2002-07-30}}</ref> In addition to sprouting new plants from seeds, rootstocks can also produce new plants in the fall from the basal [[meristem]]. When these detach the following spring, they may form a new plant.
[[File:Cicuta douglasii leaf detail.jpg|thumb|alt=Cicuta douglasii, close-up showing part of leaf.|Leaf detail, showing distinctive venation (see text).]]
== Distribution and habitat ==
Water hemlock is most abundant in [[British Columbia]],<ref name="weedsbc" /> and is indigenous to [[North America]],<ref name="block" /> where it grows primarily from the base of the [[Rocky Mountains]] to the Pacific coast, stretching from [[Alaska]] all the way to [[California]]. Water requirements limit this plant from inhabiting open rangelands.<ref name="block" /> It grows in wet places such as marshes, stream banks, slough margins, ditches, meadows, and wet pastures.<ref name="weedsbc" /><ref name="agfood" />  

==Toxicity==
{{main|Cicuta toxicity}}

The main distinguishing characteristic of western water hemlock is its toxicity.  [[Cicutoxin]] is the [[toxin]] that is produced, making water hemlock the most [[poisonous plant]] in North America.<ref name="Schep">{{cite journal |vauthors=Schep LJ, Slaughter RJ, Becket G, Beasley DM |title=Poisoning due to water hemlock |journal=Clin Toxicol |volume=47 |issue=4 |pages=270–8 |date=April 2009 |pmid=19514873 |doi=10.1080/15563650902904332|s2cid=21855822 }}</ref>  Cicutoxin is a yellowish liquid that is prevalent in the roots. This [[unsaturated alcohol]] has a major impact on the central nervous system of animals. Early symptoms of cicutoxin poisoning include excessive salivation, frothing at the mouth, nervousness, and incoordination. These symptoms can progress to tremors, muscular weakness, seizures and respiratory failure.<ref name="block" /> Ingestion of green materials of western water hemlock in amounts equivalent to about 0.1% of a person's body weight can even lead to death.<ref name="minag">{{cite web|url=http://www.agf.gov.bc.ca/cropprot/whemlock.htm|title=Western water hemlock|publisher=Ministry of Agriculture and Lands, Government of British Columbia|date=2005-07-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050829065145/http://www.agf.gov.bc.ca/cropprot/whemlock.htm|archive-date=2005-08-29}}</ref> In addition to being extremely hazardous to humans, this plant has an enormous impact on animals. As little as 0.2–0.5% body weight for sheep, 0.1% body weight for cattle, 0.5% body weight for horses, and 0.3% body weight for swine can be lethal. Death can occur within fifteen minutes of ingesting the toxin. It is one of the first plants to emerge in springtime, and has a very appealing odor.<ref name="block" /> These characteristics, along with the fact that it grows in moist areas, make the plant very attractive, but deadly, to grazing animals.
